displayQuote: Science is organized knowledge. Wisdom is organized life

meta.title: Who really said "Science is organized knowledge. Wisdom is organized life"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No. Immanuel Kant never wrote it. Herbert Spencer coined the first half in 1854; Will Durant fused the two-part line while paraphrasing Kant in The Story of Philosophy.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Science is organized knowledge. Wisdom is organized life'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Kant. Herbert Spencer coined half of it in 1854; Will Durant welded the two-part adage together while explaining Kant. The Kant label starts with a 1969 filler item.

answer.label: Not Immanuel Kant — Will Durant, echoing Herbert Spencer
answer.sourceLine: Immanuel Kant never wrote or said this — Quote Investigator found no German or English citation for it in his work. The first half, “Science is organized knowledge,” belongs to Herbert Spencer (1854). The two-part line as quoted was assembled by Will Durant while paraphrasing Kant in The Story of Philosophy; QI tentatively credits Durant with the combined adage. The “Kant” label first surfaces in a 1969 newspaper filler.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from
source.excerpt: Sensation is unorganized stimulus, perception is organized sensation, conception is organized perception, science is organized knowledge, wisdom is organized life: each is a greater degree of order, and sequence, and unity.
trail: 1854: Herbert Spencer publishes “Science is organized knowledge” in “The Art of Education,” The North British Review; he reprints it in Education (1861).
1926: Will Durant, explaining Kant in The Story of Philosophy, builds the ladder ending “science is organized knowledge, wisdom is organized life” — his own paraphrase, not a translation of Kant.
1969: The San Diego Union runs both clauses together under Kant’s name in a “Worth Repeating” filler — the earliest Kant attribution QI could find.
Today: quote sites still stamp the line on Kant, though QI tentatively credits Durant with the combined adage and Spencer with the first half.
source.excerptNote: Will Durant’s hierarchy in The Story of Philosophy, written to convey Kant’s spirit rather than to translate him. Popular quotation pulls the last two clauses out and reattributes the pair to Kant. As Durant noted, his Kant chapter used few direct quotations because Kant was “hardly intelligible to the beginner.”
source.rightsHolder: Estate of Will Durant / Simon & Schuster
source.rightsNote: The first half (“Science is organized knowledge”) is Herbert Spencer’s 1854 wording and is public domain. But the quotation as worded — with “wisdom is organized life” — is Will Durant’s from The Story of Philosophy, whose text (Durant died 1981) remains under active copyright by his estate and publisher Simon & Schuster; treat the combined line as in-copyright.

author.name: Will Durant
author.heading: Will Durant
author.bio: Will Durant was an American historian and philosopher best known for The Story of Philosophy (1926), a runaway best-seller that popularized the great thinkers for general readers, and for the 11-volume The Story of Civilization, co-written with his wife Ariel. Because his aim was to render dense thinkers “intelligible to the beginner,” his prose often distills a philosopher’s ideas into crisp aphorisms of his own — which is exactly how this line, meant to echo Kant, ended up pinned on Kant instead.

misattribution.heading: How Kant got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a classic “magnet name” misattribution: a clever, orderly-sounding line about wisdom drifts to the most famous philosopher in the room. Two different writers actually built it.

items.why: Kant died in 1804. Quote Investigator found no citation in German or English showing he ever wrote or said this; the line surfaces only long after his death.
“Science is organized knowledge” is Spencer’s, from “The Art of Education” (1854), reprinted in his 1861 book Education.
Durant welded “wisdom is organized life” onto Spencer’s phrase while paraphrasing Kant in The Story of Philosophy; QI credits him with the pairing.

misattribution.truthLine: Spencer coined half of it, Durant wrote the memorable second half while channeling Kant, and a 1969 newspaper filler handed the whole thing to Kant — where it has stuck ever since.

context.heading: Why the mix-up is so sticky
lead: The line reads like Kant because Durant meant it to. His whole method in The Story of Philosophy was to boil a difficult thinker down to something a beginner could hold onto, and his ladder — sensation, perception, conception, science, wisdom — is a tidy gloss on Kant’s architecture of the mind. Strip away the surrounding paragraph and you get an epigram that sounds like it was lifted straight from the Königsberg philosopher.

Add a genuine Herbert Spencer phrase for the first half, and the quotation carries two layers of real philosophical pedigree — just not Kant’s. That is exactly the recipe for a durable misattribution.
context.pull: Durant wrote it to sound like Kant. It worked a little too well.
